title: The nodes are the specification
text:
The specification is the set of its nodes.

Whatever is generated from them — a readable export (for example, in markdown), the map, the instructions an agent reads — is regenerated after every change to them and never edited, and nothing is ever read back from it into the specification. What is generated from them into the system's code — its types and runtime checks (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), and what a project's own generators write (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze) — waits for its nodes instead: it is regenerated only once every node it is generated from is approved, and until then no commit changes it.

Where a generated copy is kept, it is checked against what the nodes produce, unless it waits.
reason:
A structure a schema can check is hard for a person to read, so a readable copy is needed; but a copy that is edited, fed back into the nodes or left behind them would be a second version of the rules: sooner or later one version would change and the other not, and whoever read the unchanged one would implement a rule that no longer holds. Regenerated by the tools at every change and checked against the nodes, a copy is a view of the one source rather than a second one.

Code generated from a node is part of the system: regenerated from a draft node, it would implement what none of the node's owners has approved (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug). Waiting, it lets a change to the node be committed before its approval, as a change to any rule is; and since no commit changes it meanwhile, it is still never edited. A copy that waits is left behind its nodes only until every one of them is approved, and its lag is reported meanwhile (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh), so that nobody takes it for current.

title: The structure of the specification is defined by its schema
text: The structure of every node and every file of the specification is defined by its schema: the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines, with the extension a project's own guidelines add to it. The extension may add only kinds of node (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2), fields of an existing kind, which the nodes of the SpecSheriff guidelines need not hold, and properties of a file or of a link, and changes no definition the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines holds. A file that does not match the schema is refused, and the refusal names the field that is wrong. Why each part of the structure is as it is, is written in the schema beside it.
reason:
A structure stated in prose can be broken without anyone noticing; stated as a schema that every file is checked against, it cannot. The schema is therefore the only description of the structure, and a rule that names a part of it, to say what that part means, is compared with it by machine.

A project needs kinds, fields and properties the SpecSheriff guidelines cannot foresee, and they are held as the shared ones are only where they stand in the schema every file is checked against. An extension that changes no definition of the shared schema keeps every structure the SpecSheriff guidelines define the same in every project, so a tool or a reader relying on one is never wrong there.

title: A node is one rule, and a section holds rules
text: One numbered rule is one node, and its continuation paragraphs, tables and code blocks belong to that node rather than standing beside it. A section is a container of rules: its text states what the section is responsible for and requires nothing, since every requirement is a rule, and it holds at least one rule — a RecordType, a term node or a node of a project's own kind (§s-vsh384ybt4w25a2) counts as one, and the rules of the sections inside it count as its own. A section whose rules have all gone is deleted, and every link and citation naming it is moved to the node that now holds its matter, or removed.
reason: A rule's parts only make sense together. Splitting them into nodes of their own would invent a second set of locations for fragments nothing can cite. A requirement written into a section's text is a rule nobody can cite, name in a SpecTag or check on its own, and a section with no rule states a responsibility nothing in the code answers to. A RecordType, a term node and a node of a project's own kind each state on their own what must hold, as a rule does — a RecordType the shape of its data, a term what its word means in every rule that uses it, a node of a project's own kind what its kind is declared for — and each is cited by its sid and named by SpecTags, so a section holding one holds a requirement.

title: A node is cited by its sid, and its location names where it is in the specification
reason: A reference to a place breaks whenever the place changes. A specification that grows is reordered, and its rules move between domains, for as long as it grows. A sid is not a place: moving a node changes its location, never its sid, so no reference holding the sid breaks. The location stays where a person reads, computed so that it can never disagree with where the node is.

title: What a node's status says
reason:
An approved status claims that one of the node's owners agreed to what it now states. A status that survived a rewrite would certify words nobody approved. A draft node asks for no code (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug) and tells its owners that it waits for their approval.

A change of owners changes who reads a part, not what a rule states. An owner leaving, or a node moving, takes back nothing that was agreed. Links, metadata and what is built from other nodes are not what an owner approved, and they change as the specification grows around a rule.

A withdrawal gives no agreement in anyone's name: it only makes a node a draft, as a change to its wording by anyone does. So whoever finds an approved rule wrong can keep any further change to its code or its tests from being committed (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug) without waiting for its owners. The withdrawal names whoever made it, which tells the owners whom to ask. A project takes the SpecSheriff guidelines as they were approved where they are written (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab), so their approval is not the project's to withdraw. Whether the rule that approves the specification is approved decides how strictly the checks hold all code and tests, which is the specification's owners' decision (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2).

title: The status of a section and of a domain's header
text: The status of a section is built from the nodes under it that are no section: approved where every one of them is approved, and draft otherwise. The status of a domain's header is built the same way from every node of the domain but the header itself. Nobody approves a section or a header itself, nor a header's level and where its code is. The status is built anew after every change to the specification and never written by hand.
reason: A section and a domain's header require nothing (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg, §s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr): what they state, the nodes under them state, so their own words leave an owner nothing to agree to. A header's level is one of those the project's own guidelines list (§s-nkyty4dy9x2v2a4), in a rule the specification's owners approve. Where its code is says where to look, not what must hold. Built from the nodes under it, the status shows at a glance which parts of the specification wait for their owners. Built anew after every change, it never falls behind those nodes (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j).

title: Only its owners approve a node
text:
The specification has owners, one or several. A domain (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7) or a section may have owners of its own, who take the place of the owners above for every node within it.

A node is approved by one of its owners and by nobody else. An approval names whoever gave it.

An agent working for one of a node's owners approves the node in that owner's name where its wording changes only:

- to state what one of its owners approved in another node;
- by a replacement that changes no meaning, such as a renamed term or path.

The agent reports each such approval to that owner, who may withdraw it.
reason:
An approval means that someone who answers for a rule has agreed to what it states, so it is theirs to give. Named, whoever approved is compared with the node's owners and can be asked later. Owners of domains and sections divide the reading as the specification is divided, so that it can grow beyond what one person reads. The owners of one part share its reading, and each of them answers for all of it.

A node whose wording only states what one of its owners approved in another node asks nothing its owners have not agreed to. A replacement that changes no meaning states nothing new. Shown again, either would spend the owners' attention on no decision. An agent working for an owner already acts in that owner's name and reports to them as it works. The report lets the owner see that the change was only that, and withdraw the approval where it was not.

title: A draft node is not implemented
text: A node is implemented only once it is approved. Before a domain's implementation begins, the domain is reviewed whole; where the implementation then finds a node silent or wrong, that node is changed and reviewed when the problem is found, not later.
reason: The specification is expected to be incomplete. Implementing a draft node fills its gap with a guess made in the code, which the specification then does not hold; reviewing the node at once keeps the answer in the specification.

title: Removal goes through the archive when an approval was ever given
text:
A node an approval was ever given for is moved to the archive when it is removed, together with the reason for its removal and the sid of the node that replaces it, if one does. A section, a domain's header and a node no approval was ever given for are deleted outright, whatever cited them.

A node may later be deleted from the archive.
reason:
A rule one of its owners approved is one the code may implement, and a later change to its wording does not undo what was implemented from it, so its removal is worth keeping for a time. Kept in its last wording, it can be restored if its removal is undone. And it is a record for the decisions taken: an approved rule that had to go, a rule of the base above all, most often shows a logic or an approach that was mistaken, which later work has to understand and take into account, as it would a list of the defects found.

Nothing guarantees how long the archive keeps a node, so a link or a citation naming an archived node breaks when the node is deleted, and the checks refuse it until it is removed. A node no approval was ever given for was never implemented, since no SpecTag may name it, and archived it would only bury the rules that had to go under wording nobody approved. A section and a domain's header require nothing and nobody approves them (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs), so no code was implemented from them and their removal keeps nothing worth restoring.

title: A decision lives on the rule it settled
text: A decision records what was settled about a rule. It is kept in that rule's metadata, never as a document of its own. A decision usually changes the rule's wording; a procedural one changes none.
reason: A decision is not specification but the history of one rule, and it is read beside that rule. The procedural kind would otherwise leave no trace, because nothing in the wording shows it. And the number of decisions on one rule measures how well it was written: a rule that keeps collecting them was written badly.

title: Work put off lives on the node it concerns
text: Work put off that concerns one node is kept in that node's metadata, as an item of its todos. An item holds the day the work was put off, who its author is and what is to be done. It is never kept in a comment on the node or in a document of its own. A problem of the default implementation set aside is a rule of the technical debt instead (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw). An item is removed once it is done or given up. Every item of the todos across the specification can be listed at once, the newest first, each with the node it stands on.
reason: Work put off is read beside the node it concerns, as a decision is, so whoever opens the node sees what still waits on it. Its date orders the listing, and its author tells the reader whom to ask. Kept in a comment or a document, it is missed by the listing. An item left once done or given up shows work waiting that no longer waits. Listed together, the items show what waits across the specification. The newest stand first: each older item was weighed at every listing since, a new one at none.

title: A rule and its reason are held apart
text: A node's text states what must hold, except a rule of the technical debt, which describes a problem as it stands (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw). Why it must hold is kept in a separate field of the same node and is not part of the requirement. When a rule is revised, its reason is checked first: a rule whose reason no longer holds is removed, not reworded.
reason: Mixed in one text, a rule is long and a reviewer cannot tell which half is being asserted. And a reason that has stopped holding is the surest sign the rule should go — which nobody sees while the reason is buried inside the requirement.

title: What the specification governs
text: The specification describes the system — its logic, its architecture and everything the system is made of — and governs one process only: how the specification itself is kept, changed and implemented. A rule that tries to govern anything else is dropped, and so is a rule that states the obvious.
reason: A rule governing what nobody here controls decides nothing: an agent that has never read an instruction cannot be stopped by it, however many are written. Duplication and drift are fought by structure — one model, a generated export, links a checker resolves — not by prohibitions. A rule stating the obvious costs a reading and decides nothing either.

title: The specification holds its content; the code implements it
text: The specification holds its content and the code implements it, never the reverse. A rule does not hand what it states to a declaration in the code: a set of states, a list of members, a table of routes is described in the specification, and the code is checked against it. A rule that sends its reader to a source file for its content is a defect, repaired when that rule is revised.
reason: A specification that leaves a list in the code and names only its meaning cannot say what the system is, and a copy of that list written beside it in prose goes stale with nothing noticing. Held in the specification and checked against the code, the content is in one place and the disagreement is found by a machine.

title: A list's member may be an object
text: Each member of a list a rule holds is a primitive value or an object. In an object, the property the list names holds the member's value, and the other properties, each a primitive value, a list or an object, hold what is stated of that value.
reason: What is stated of a value, held in that value's own object, is never taken for what is stated of another; the named property stays where the value is declared, so the members are read, and compared with their declaration, the same whatever else they hold.

title: The base specification names no technology
text: A rule of the base specification states what the system does, never how the default implementation does it: it names no programming language, library, store, protocol, command or file path. How it is done, and any part of a rule that depends on it, is described in the technical appendix. A technology may be named by example, in brackets, where the rule does not depend on it.
reason: The same rules can then be implemented on another stack, with an appendix of its own, without editing a single rule; and a rule that names its tools goes stale when they change, although what the system does has not.

title: Of a user interface the base states what it shows, not how it looks
text: Of a user interface, the base specification states what a user can rely on in any instance: what is shown, what it means, in what order, in which states, and what the user can do. How it looks and is built — placement, size, colour, icon, the kind of control, where a state is kept — is described in the technical appendix.
reason: The same rules can then be given another look with an appendix of its own; and a rule that names its look goes stale when the look changes, although what the user can rely on has not.

title: The base specification holds no figure of one instance
text: The base specification holds no figure measured on an instance — a population, a rate, a duration observed there. A threshold a rule needs is stated by the method an instance measures it with, and its value is a setting of the technical appendix.
reason: A figure belongs to the instance it was measured on and to the day it was measured, so every other instance would pass or fail the rule by accident.

title: The technical appendix stands beside the base specification
text:
The technical appendix describes how this repository builds the system — its stack, how each domain is built and how the user interface looks — in the detail an instance needs to repeat it; every part but it and the guidelines is the base specification.

It is no domain and stands at no level, beside the domains as contracts does, with a section for each domain it implements, under that domain's name, one for the stack, and, while any problem is set aside, one for its technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

It never contradicts a rule of the base specification but extends and refines it: a rule too narrow for an implementation is widened in the base, its detail going to the technical appendix.

A node of the appendix describes how the nodes of the base specification it implements are to be carried out, in enough detail to be read only one way — exact values, examples and the edge cases of that implementation — and never restates what they state. Each of its nodes but a section, which requires nothing (§s-7445ahgjck2aefg), implements at least one node of the base specification, except a choice covering the whole system, which stands in the section of the stack, and except the technical debt (§s-2r7k2aeyusgy6fw).

An instance changes the technical appendix for itself, and what instances vary within it is a setting, described with its default.
reason:
The base specification stays stable while an implementation adapts to an instance's infrastructure and requirements, so only the technical appendix changes with an instance.

A part allowed to contradict the base would leave the base binding nowhere, since no rule could be relied on without reading the implementation too. Read beside the nodes it implements, an appendix node restating them would be a second copy, and a copy drifts from what it copies; how a rule is carried out has no other home, since the base names no technology, and described less exactly it would leave a choice to whoever implements it, which the code would then hold and the specification would not.

It is no subject area of the system but the way every one of them is built, which no level can place. A node bound to the rule it implements is found when that rule changes and is read beside it, and divided as the base is, the implementation of a rule is looked for in one place.

The problems set aside are read as one list, so they stand in one section, which spans the domains as the stack does, and a problem is not how a rule is carried out but where carrying it out falls short.

The repository holds nothing of any one instance, so what one instance chooses within the appendix is a setting, not a rule.

title: The technical debt holds the problems of the default implementation set aside
text: The section of the technical debt holds rules alone, each describing one problem of the default implementation as it stands and refining the nodes the default implementation falls short of there, one of the base specification at least; where the problem lies in a technology the default implementation uses, its rule names the version of that technology it was seen in. Standing there is the whole of the decision to set the problem aside: its rule carries no reason, no decision records it, and the change that solves the problem removes the rule.
reason: A problem set aside needs a place where it is stated, or it is forgotten, or kept as a task nobody means to do. Every problem there stands for the one reason that the specification's owners judged it not worth solving now, so a reason or a decision of its own would only repeat its standing. Described as it stands and bound to the nodes it concerns, it tells whoever repeats an instance, or reads those nodes, what the implementation does not do; a problem in a technology may be solved by a later version of it while nothing here changes, and the version it was seen in lets a reader tell. Left standing once solved, it would describe a shortfall that no longer exists.
